Pandemic, epidemic, endemic.  What is the difference?  Since I am not in the medical field I needed to look these terms up to be sure I had a handle on the differences and similarities of these three terms.  According to the old standby Merriam-Webster (and selectively quoting to fit the purpose of this column and keep it shorter), this is what I came up with;

Pandemic -adjective

1:occurring over a wide geographic area(such as multiple countries or continents) and typically affecting a significant proportion of the population

2: characterized by verywidespread growth or extent

Pandemic -noun

1: anoutbreak of a disease that occurs over a wide geographic area(such as multiple countries or continents) and typically affects a significant proportion of the population

2: an outbreak or product of sudden rapid spread, growth, or development

OK, so a pandemic is a disease that affects a wide area and has a lot of infected people, which is easy enough.

Epidemic-adjective

1: affecting or tending to affect a disproportionately large number of individuals within a population, community, or region at the same time

2a:excessivelyprevalent

3: characterized by verywidespread growthor extent :of, relating to, or constituting an epidemic

Epidemic-noun

1: anoutbreak of disease that spreads quickly and affects many individuals at the same time

2: an outbreak or product of sudden rapid spread, growth, or development

A bit more difficult to put my finger on, but I suppose it means an Epidemic is a Pandemic when it affects a wider area and a lot more people get it; or it is more prevalent, am I right?  There are not a lot of differences and it seems that one more often than not reference the same thing.

Now we get to throw a monkey wrench into the mix and figure out what an endemic is.

Endemic-adjective

1a: belonging or native to a particular people or country

b: characteristic of orprevalent in a particular field, area, or environment

2:restricted or peculiar to a locality or region

Endemic-noun

: an organism that is restricted or peculiar to a locality or region : an endemic organism

Perhaps I may require a bit more help with this one as it seems to indicate specifically that it is a situation, in this case a pandemic that is limited to a particular region or peoples.  So an epidemic of endemic illnesses makes for a pandemic?  Please excuse me if I do not understand it correctly, but that is what I get out of it.  But that is not really of any great concern with todays discussion except that there are stories of various states dropping the pandemic label as it appears that the fake Plandemic err, I meant Pandemic  is waning while the dictators  errr, I meant Governors that have grown to love their tyrannical grasp on absolute power and control so they then declare the plandemic an Endemic for their area.  Using the noun description of Endemic it appears to be something (in this case a pandemic) restricted to their own peculiar  umm, I meant particular state, or at least an excuse to maintain pandemic control mechanisms in place even though they may be relaxing somewhat from the harsh but ILLEGAL rules a bit.

Why would I even bring this distinction of terms up?  Well, because they did.  And by they I mean the dictators involved.  The actual Cov/SARS farce lasted only a year with this second year being mostly the result of the kill shots and normal flu and cold season, which is waning all by itself regardless of the attempts to mangle the truth enough to keep the farce going.

But theres no consensus on the conditions for meeting this benchmark. By this broad definition,endemicity doesnt necessarily mean a disease is rare or common, mild or severe. For example,infection rates can still be high; they just have to remain static. Malaria, which is endemic in dozens of countries, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa, killed more than six hundred thousand people in 2020.That sounds like they are not producing enough Ivermectin to go around and it would be a safe bet that is on purpose.
